issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s construction materially alters an accommodation only when it makes a substantial change to the building’s character, form, or structure.
material_facts: The tenant placed a six-foot partition in a hall without a foundation and without reaching the ceiling; it could be removed without damage and served to divide the hall for convenient use.
The disputed tin shed stood on adjoining open land, was made with temporary materials, and could be removed without damage; an existing shed had merely been extended.
The lower appellate court found that these constructions did not substantially change the accommodation, but the High Court treated them as material alterations.
issues.conclusion: Neither the partition nor the tin shed materially altered the accommodation, so the statutory ground for eviction was not established.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “materially altered” means a substantial change in the character, form, or structure of a building without destroying its identity. The court considers the nature and character of the construction and the extent of the change, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation was let. Minor alterations for convenient use do not qualify when the building’s form and structure remain unaffected. The Court relied on the dictionary meanings of “alter” and “materially,” Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das, S.B. Mathur v. K.P. Gupta, Dr. J.G. Gupta v. Bodh Mal, Sita Ram Sharan v. Johri Mal, and Baldev Das v. Ram Khilawan.

rule.if: eviction_claim_based_on_tenant_construction and tenant_made_unauthorized_construction and (construction_is_temporary_and_removable and not substantial_change_to_building)

predicates.eviction_claim_based_on_tenant_construct: The landlord seeks eviction on the basis of construction made or permitted by the tenant.
predicates.tenant_made_unauthorized_construction: The tenant made or permitted construction without the landlord’s consent.
predicates.construction_is_temporary_and_removable: The construction is temporary and can be removed without damage to the building.
predicates.substantial_change_to_building: The construction substantially changes the building’s character, form, or structure.

issues.definition: When an eviction claim concerns unauthorized tenant construction, temporary and removable work that does not substantially change the building does not produce the stated material-alteration finding.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may obtain eviction for unauthorized construction only if the tenant made or permitted the construction, did so without the landlord’s consent, and the construction materially altered the accommodation; all three requirements must be established.
material_facts: The landlord’s surviving eviction claim alleged unauthorized construction that materially altered the accommodation.
The courts found that some disputed work lacked the landlords’ consent, but the Supreme Court concluded that none of the work materially altered the accommodation.
issues.conclusion: Because material alteration was not established, the landlord was not entitled to eviction on this ground.
issues.legal_principle: The requirements that the tenant made or permitted construction, that it was made without the landlord’s consent, and that it materially altered the accommodation are cumulative. Each must be established before eviction may be decreed. Under section 14 of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952, a landlord ordinarily needs the District Magistrate’s permission to sue for eviction, but the qualifying unauthorized construction provides an exception. The decision applies the meaning of “materially altered” explained in Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das and in the Court’s discussion of the statutory language.

predicates.eviction_claim_based_on_tenant_construct: The landlord seeks eviction on the basis of construction made or permitted by the tenant.
predicates.tenant_made_or_permitted_construction: The tenant made or permitted the construction.
predicates.construction_without_landlord_consent: The construction was made without the landlord’s consent.
predicates.construction_materially_altered_accommod: The construction substantially changed the accommodation’s character, form, or structure.

issues.definition: The stated eviction consequence follows only when the eviction claim concerns tenant construction and each of the three construction-related requirements is met.

issues.legal_issue: Whether construction materially alters an accommodation requires consideration of whether it is permanent or temporary and removable.
material_facts: The partition was temporary, lacked a foundation, did not reach the ceiling, and could be removed without damage.
The tin shed was temporary, stood on open land, and could be removed without damage.
The High Court treated the temporary nature and removability of the disputed work as irrelevant to material alteration.
issues.conclusion: The permanent or temporary nature of construction is a relevant consideration; temporary work that can be removed without damage ordinarily does not affect the building’s form or structure in the same way as permanent construction.
issues.legal_principle: The nature of construction, including whether it is permanent or temporary, is relevant to deciding whether an alteration is material. Permanent construction tends to change the accommodation on a lasting basis; temporary construction that can readily be removed without damage ordinarily does not affect the building’s form or structure. The Court rejected the contrary observation in the Full Bench decision in Sita Ram Sharan v. Johri Mal and explained that Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das did not make permanence irrelevant.

predicates.material_alteration_assessment: The court is deciding whether construction materially altered an accommodation.
predicates.construction_is_temporary_and_removable: The construction is temporary and can be removed without damage to the building.

issues.definition: In a material-alteration assessment, temporary and removable construction makes its temporary and removable character relevant to the decision.

issues.legal_issue: Whether construction materially alters an accommodation is a mixed question of fact and law, and a second appellate court must apply the correct legal principles when reviewing that determination.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the partition and tin shed did not materially alter the accommodation.
The High Court reversed that determination in second appeal, treating the temporary construction as material despite its removability and the absence of substantial structural change.
The Supreme Court found no evidence supporting the High Court’s finding of substantial permanent walls and concluded that the High Court applied an incorrect approach.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in interfering with the first appellate court’s determination; its order was set aside and the first appellate court’s judgment and decree were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Findings about what construction was made are findings of fact, but whether those constructions materially alter the accommodation is a mixed question of fact and law that must be decided using the correct principles. The Court applied the material-alteration test in Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das and rejected the High Court’s reliance on the contrary observation in Sita Ram Sharan v. Johri Mal.

predicates.second_appeal_in_eviction_case: The matter is a second appeal in an eviction case.
predicates.material_alteration_is_mixed_question_of: The disputed determination concerns whether established construction materially altered the accommodation, a mixed question of fact and law.
predicates.first_appellate_court_found_no_material_: The first appellate court found that the construction did not materially alter the accommodation.
predicates.second_appellate_court_applied_incorrect: The second appellate court reversed that finding using an incorrect legal approach to material alteration.

issues.definition: A second appellate reversal is unwarranted when the first appellate court found no material alteration on a mixed question and the second appellate court used an incorrect test.
